records.sourceFile: Clinical outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament injury - Panther Symposium ACL Injury Clinical Outcomes Consensus Group.pdf

paper.citation: Svantesson E, Hamrin Senorski E, Webster KE, Karlsson J, Diermeier T, Rothrauff BB, et al. Clinical Outcomes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Clinical Outcomes Consensus Group. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;8(7):2325967120934751.
paper.abstract: A multidisciplinary international panel of ACL experts used a modified Delphi process at the 2019 Panther Symposium to agree on how clinical outcome after ACL treatment should be measured and reported. The consensus covers study planning, clinical assessment, osteoarthritis, laxity and patient-reported outcomes (PROs).
paper.tldr: Report ACL outcomes in four categories: early adverse events, PROs, graft failure or reinjury, and clinical knee function and structure. Aim for at least 2 years of follow-up with about 80% retention, describe pretreatment status, and use the IKDC-SKF as the preferred knee-specific PRO.
paper.methods: A 25-member working group discussed 13 draft statements, which were pre-voted through an online survey and then debated at an in-person meeting in June 2019. Statements needed 80% agreement; nine reached consensus, and four were excluded or merged into others. The liaisons completed a MEDLINE literature review for each final statement.
paper.findings: Consensus was reached on: an a priori power calculation (25 of 25); a pretreatment description including demographics, a knee PRO, HRQoL and preinjury sport level (statement 2 was merged, so no agreement percentage is reported); a follow-up length set by the outcome being assessed, optimally including 80% of the cohort (25 of 25); a minimum 2-year assessment covering adverse events, knee function and structure, PROs, activity level and reinjury (25 of 25); osteoarthritis assessment at 5 years; AP and rotatory laxity testing; a PRO set of one knee-specific tool, one activity scale and one HRQoL measure; the PASS; and the IKDC-SKF as the recommended knee-related measure (24 of 25).
paper.limitations: This is expert opinion built on voting and literature review, with no formal evidence grading. The symposium was industry-sponsored and many authors report industry ties. The paper itself notes gaps in the tools it recommends, including the lack of structural validity evidence for the IKDC-SKF and limited responsiveness of the KOOS after ACL injury.
paper.practicalImplications: For ACL outcome tracking, record the pretreatment knee PRO, preinjury sport or activity level (Marx scale) and HRQoL, and report knee laxity alongside PROs. Read PRO change against the MDC and MCID, and use the PASS to see whether the patient reaches an acceptable knee state.
paper.athleteDev: The paper concerns outcome reporting after ACL treatment, not training. For performance staff, it supports recording preinjury sport level and the exact knee-specific tool used, so that return-to-sport and rehab outcomes can be compared across athletes and time points.
paper.rtp: Supports a 2-year outcome battery for ACL reconstruction (clinical knee exam with laxity, IKDC-SKF, activity scale, HRQoL and reinjury history) as a reporting standard. It does not set return-to-sport criteria or timing; the paper refers readers to a separate Panther Symposium consensus on return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Commotio Cordis in 2023.pdf

paper.citation: Peng T, Trollinger Derry L, Yogeswaran V, Goldschlager NF. Commotio cordis in 2023. Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: A narrative review of commotio cordis, sudden cardiac arrest caused by blunt trauma over the heart, prompted by the 2023 collapse of an NFL player. It summarises epidemiology, registry data, mechanisms, diagnosis, management and return to play, and calls for better reporting, defibrillator access and medical cover at sports events.
paper.tldr: Commotio cordis is a rare but important cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, and survival depends on fast CPR and defibrillation. Staff should recognise it early, have AEDs and trained responders at training and games, and support better case reporting.
paper.methods: A narrative review drawing on registry reports, case series, animal models and guidelines, organised around epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, presentation, management and future directions. The authors state only that they performed an initial literature search; no search protocol or inclusion criteria are given.
paper.findings: The review describes commotio cordis as the third most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, with more than 75% of cases occurring in sport and baseball the most common sport. In the US National Commotio Cordis Registry, survival rose from 10 to 15% in early reports to 58% in a 2013 update, with 40% survival when resuscitation began within 3 minutes and 5% when it was delayed beyond 3 minutes. In swine models, ventricular fibrillation followed impacts only within a narrow window of the T wave, and AED shocks given at 1-minute intervals gave 100% survival compared with 46% at 4 minutes.
paper.limitations: A narrative review with no described search or evidence grading. Registry case counts are dated (216 as of 2012) and reporting is not standardised, so true incidence is unknown, as the authors note. The timing and projectile findings come from animal models, and several return-to-play and equipment points rest on expert opinion or on case reports.
paper.practicalImplications: Ensure AEDs are accessible within 5 minutes at organised sport events, and train coaches, staff and players in CPR and AED use. A collapse after a chest blow should prompt immediate CPR and defibrillation, and the case should be reported to a registry. Chest protectors have not been shown to prevent this in registry or swine data, so they should not be relied on, and age-appropriate safety baseballs are recommended for children up to 13 years old.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review's relevance is emergency readiness rather than training. Survival depends on CPR and AED use within minutes, so defibrillator access and staff training should cover practices as well as games.
paper.rtp: The review states that return to play after commotio cordis is decided case by case, and that implantable defibrillators have not been recommended for survivors, since no data show later sudden death risk in them. It gives no return-to-play criteria, and it notes that recurrence is extremely rare, with one reported suspected case.

records.sourceFile: Commotio Cordis in Sudden Cardiac Death in the Young - A State-of-the-Art Review.pdf

paper.citation: Salzillo C, Marzullo A. Commotio Cordis in Sudden Cardiac Death in the Young: A State-of-the-Art Review. Rev. Cardiovasc. Med. 2025;26(9):43357.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of commotio cordis, a rare but often fatal cause of sudden cardiac death in young people, particularly athletes exposed to non-penetrating chest impact. The authors summarize pathophysiology, epidemiology, postmortem diagnosis, medicolegal issues and prevention, including AED access, CPR training and chest protectors.
paper.tldr: Commotio cordis is a rare, often fatal arrhythmia caused by a chest blow in a young person without structural heart disease, and survival depends on immediate CPR and defibrillation. The evidence that chest protectors prevent it is debated, so the review's practical emphasis is AED access, CPR training and emergency planning.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The paper does not describe a search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal method, and reports no original data. It draws on autopsy series, national registries, a systematic review of 334 documented cases, and experimental and biomechanical studies.
paper.findings: The authors report approximately 15-25 US cases per year and state that the true incidence is likely underestimated. They report that 36% of 334 documented cases occurred outside sport, with higher mortality in non-sport events (88% vs 66%), attributed to lower bystander CPR (27% vs 97%) and defibrillation (17% vs 81%) rates. They state that defibrillation within three minutes can raise survival above 70%, and cite a study showing that not all commercially available chest protectors offer sufficient protection.
paper.limitations: The review has no stated search method, so the choice of sources cannot be checked. Post-mortem diagnosis depends on autopsy protocols that often omit genetic testing, which the authors note makes case counts difficult. The section on delayed-onset arrhythmias and the efficacy ratings in Table 2 are not tied to a described method or to clinical outcome data in the text.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff responsible for contact-sport athletes should confirm AED availability and CPR-trained personnel at training and competition venues, since the authors identify these as the most effective measures for survival. Any collapse after a chest blow should prompt immediate CPR and defibrillation. If chest protectors are used, the review points to certified standards such as ND200, but it does not establish that protectors prevent commotio cordis.
paper.athleteDev: The review has no performance-training content. Its relevant point is emergency preparedness in contact and collision sport, specifically AED access, CPR-trained staff and emergency action plans.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport and gives no return-to-play criteria. It notes that subacute post-traumatic arrhythmias may need prolonged ECG surveillance, cardiac imaging and genetic testing even without symptoms, but it does not say when an athlete may return after a chest-trauma event.

records.sourceFile: Comparative Electromyographic Activity of Hamstrings During Sprinting Versus Strengthening Exercises - Implications for Injury Prevention.pdf

paper.citation: Moiroux-Sahraoui A, Mazeas J, Bener E, Bouzekraoui Alaoui I, Douryang M, Forelli F. Comparative Electromyographic Activity of Hamstrings During Sprinting Versus Strengthening Exercises: Implications for Injury Prevention. Cureus. 2024;16(8):e66370.
paper.abstract: Pilot study comparing hamstring EMG activity in 15 sprint-exposed field athletes during maximal 30-m sprints, Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) and high-speed isokinetic knee flexion at 300 deg/s. Sprinting produced the highest mean hamstring activity, followed by NHE and then isokinetic exercise, and the authors suggest that sprinting be combined with NHE in prevention and rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: In 15 sprint-exposed athletes, 30-m sprinting produced higher hamstring EMG than Nordic hamstring exercise, which in turn exceeded fast isokinetic knee flexion. This is a small pilot that measured muscle activation only, not injury or strength outcomes, so it supports exercise selection as a starting point rather than proof of prevention.
paper.methods: Single-group pilot with all exercises performed by each participant in randomized order. Surface EMG from the semitendinosus and biceps femoris was normalized to a prone isometric MVIC and compared with two-tailed Student's t-tests, with a one-sided Wilcoxon test also reported for one comparison.
paper.findings: Mean hamstring EMG was 0.48 ± 0.19 during sprinting, 0.32 ± 0.09 during NHE and 0.25 ± 0.07 during isokinetic flexion. Sprinting exceeded NHE for the biceps femoris (p < 0.01) and the two-muscle mean (p = 0.02), but not the semitendinosus (NS). NHE exceeded isokinetic flexion for the semitendinosus (p = 0.03) and the mean (p = 0.02), but not the biceps femoris (NS). Sprinting exceeded isokinetic flexion for all muscle measures (p < 0.01).
paper.limitations: The text gives n = 15 in the methods, abstract and Table 1 but n = 10 in the limitations, and states that only males were studied while Table 1 reports 13 male participants out of 15. The conclusions say the single-muscle differences were not significant, which conflicts with Tables 2-4 (for example ST p = 0.03 and BF p < 0.01). The reported BMI (13.85 ± 8.28 kg/m2) is implausibly low for adult athletes, set and repetition counts differ between the abstract and methods, the MVIC is introduced as a quadriceps test but described as a prone hamstring test, and EMG is described as normalized to MVIC yet reported in microvolts. The sample size calculation called for 381 participants, the authors acknowledge a 25% margin of error, and fatigue and electrode variability were not controlled.
paper.practicalImplications: When the goal is high hamstring muscle activity, this pilot suggests sprinting and NHE load the hamstrings more than fast isokinetic knee flexion, so isokinetic work should not be the main choice for that purpose. Because the study measured EMG amplitude only, it supports including sprint exposure alongside NHE, but it does not show that either exercise lowers injury rates.
paper.athleteDev: In this pilot, high-speed sprinting produced more hamstring EMG than NHE or fast isokinetic flexion, which suggests sprint work as a high-intensity hamstring stimulus. The study did not measure force, speed or sprint performance, so it cannot rank these exercises for performance gain.
paper.rtp: All participants were healthy athletes with no hamstring injury in the previous six months, so the study cannot show which exercises are safe or effective for an injured athlete returning to sport. It may serve as a reference for muscle activation during rehabilitation planning, but it does not provide evidence about recovery, re-injury risk or return-to-play readiness.

records.sourceFile: Comparative analysis of treatment strategies for groin injuries in athletes - Effects on successful recovery and recurrence of sports conditions – A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: de Castro Fernandes JV, Pedrinelli A, Rubio-Arias JÁ. Comparative analysis of treatment strategies for groin injuries in athletes: Effects on successful recovery and recurrence of sports conditions - A systematic review. Apunts Sports Medicine. 2025;60:100481.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of 30 studies (1,931 athletes) comparing surgical and conservative treatments for groin and adductor pain in athletes, with return to sport and recurrence as the main outcomes. The authors propose a stepped strategy that starts with shockwave therapy, manual therapy or exercise, with surgery considered if there is no improvement after 3 to 6 months.
paper.tldr: Across 30 studies with 1,931 athletes, surgical procedures such as adductor tenotomy and selective partial adductor release were reported to return most athletes to sport, and shockwave and manual therapy were linked to faster return in single studies. The authors propose 3 to 6 months of conservative care before surgery, but the included studies are heterogeneous and 12 of 30 were rated low quality.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and pre-registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023430694), with AMSTAR used for methodological quality. Searches of PubMed-MEDLINE, Web of Science and Cochrane Library ran from inception to 30 April 2023, identifying 1,296 records, 86 full texts and 30 included studies. Included studies were case-control studies or case series with n of at least 10, published from 2005 in English, Spanish or Portuguese, and were rated with the Downs and Black scale by two reviewers.
paper.findings: The authors summarize surgical return-to-sport success at around 75-80%. Individual studies reported about 75% return to previous level after adductor and/or rectus abdominis tenotomy, 42 of 43 athletes returning after selective partial release of the long adductor (mean 9.21 weeks), and 80% good or excellent results after adductor tenotomy with or without hernioplasty in a 155-athlete study. Shockwave therapy was associated with earlier return to football (p = 0.048), and manual therapy with a shorter time to return than exercise therapy (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks, p = 0.043). Eighteen studies were rated high quality and 12 low quality (mean score 16.6, SD 5.6).
paper.limitations: The review has no pooled analysis and mixes injury sites, treatments and follow-up periods, and 13 studies did not specify the type of pubalgia. Recurrence, named in the title, is reported for only a few studies. The abstract describes a qualitative analysis while the results describe a statistical analysis, the text sets high quality as above 16 points while Table 2 rates scores of 16 as high, the roughly 75% tenotomy return rate comes from two studies the review rated low quality, and a randomized trial is included although inclusion was limited to case-control studies or case series. The authors also note possible publication bias, which they do not quantify.
paper.practicalImplications: For athletes with persistent groin pain, the review supports starting with conservative care such as shockwave therapy, manual therapy or exercise, and considering surgery if there is no improvement after 3 to 6 months, as the authors propose. The authors stress that the choice between surgical approaches should follow an individual assessment of injury severity and response to conservative treatment.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not address training load or performance enhancement. It reports return-to-play rates, pain and functional scores after treatment rather than measured sport-performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Return to sport is the review's main focus. The reported return rates (about 75% to 98% in individual surgical studies) and times to return (about 9 to 17 weeks in individual studies) can inform expectations, but they come from heterogeneous, mostly uncontrolled series. The stepped algorithm is the authors' proposal and has not been validated.

records.sourceFile: Comparing Time to Recovery Between Initial and Repeat Concussion in Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Wright BS, Dykowski S, Bretzin AC, et al. Comparing Time to Recovery Between Initial and Repeat Concussion in Athletes. Clin J Sport Med. 2024;00:1-7.
paper.abstract: Retrospective review of 50 athletes treated at an interdisciplinary concussion clinic, comparing time to return-to-sport clearance after first versus second (primary) and first versus last (secondary) concussions. Time to recovery did not differ between initial and repeat concussions, and the authors conclude that recovery was not longer after repeat injury in these athletes.
paper.tldr: In 50 athletes treated at one concussion clinic, time to return-to-sport clearance did not differ between a first and a repeat concussion once initial symptom severity and time to first visit were accounted for. Earlier clinic presentation and lower initial SCAT symptom scores were associated with faster recovery.
paper.methods: Retrospective review of electronic medical records for athletes with more than one concussion who first attended a sports neurology clinic within 30 days of injury (2016 to 2020). Time to recovery was compared between first and second concussions (primary) and first and last concussions (secondary) using Cox regression, adjusted for time to initial visit and SCAT symptom severity, with sensitivity analyses by visit timing and interval between injuries.
paper.findings: Median days to recovery were 42 after first, 34 after second and 34 after last concussion, and the difference was not statistically significant. Multivariable HRs were 1.02 (95% CI 0.65-1.62, P = 0.92) for second vs first and 1.01 (95% CI 0.64-1.62, P = 0.91) for last vs first. Longer time to initial clinic visit and higher SCAT symptom number and severity were each associated with slower recovery, while age, sex, concussion history and loss of consciousness were not.
paper.limitations: The observational, retrospective design cannot establish causality, and the data reflect routine clinical documentation across several providers and years, with recovery dates tied to clinic visit timing. The sample is small, 19 of 105 injuries occurred outside sport, and only 7 patients had three or more concussions. The text reports a univariate injury-number result of HR 1.39, P = 0.008 while stating injury number was not associated with recovery, and Table 3 lists HR 1.39 (P = 0.24) for male sex; the text also gives HR 1.02, P = 0.92 for the multivariable first vs last model where Table 4 and the abstract give HR 1.01, P = 0.91. This record uses the Table 4 values.
paper.practicalImplications: A repeat concussion should not be assumed to lengthen recovery on injury number alone in this clinic's experience. At the first visit, prompt assessment and SCAT symptom scoring matter, since earlier presentation and lower initial symptom severity were associated with faster recovery.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not address training or performance outcomes. Its only performance-adjacent content is time to return-to-sport clearance after concussion.
paper.rtp: Time to return-to-sport clearance is the main outcome. Once initial symptom burden and time to first visit are considered, the study does not support a longer recovery after a repeat concussion. It cannot set return-to-play criteria, because clearance dates were set by treating physicians in one clinic.

records.sourceFile: Comparing return to play protocols after sports related concussion among international sporting organisations.pdf

paper.citation: Prock M, O'Sullivan DM, Tiernan S. Comparing return to play protocols after sports related concussion among international sporting organisations. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: Comparison of return-to-play protocols and medical rules of 12 international sporting organisations in combat, contact and collision sports, accessed through official websites. Six organisations published their own protocol, step counts were similar, initial rest and minimum time to return varied widely, and none reflected the 2023 CISG consensus statement at the time of the review.
paper.tldr: Of 12 international sporting organisations in combat, contact and collision sports, only six published their own return-to-play protocol, and minimum times to return ranged from 5 to 180 days. None of the accessible protocols had been updated to the 2023 CISG consensus statement when the documents were reviewed.
paper.methods: Structured document review (the authors call it a commentary) of concussion guidelines and medical rules from 12 of 14 eligible organisations, retrieved from official websites and Google searches on 9 September 2023 using defined keywords, and screened for concussion terms. Content was extracted into a spreadsheet under seven categories: initial rest, number of steps, sport-specific training, resistance training, medical clearance, minimum time to return, and accelerated pathways. No outcome data were analysed.
paper.findings: Six organisations published an RTP protocol, three (FIH, WL, WT) uploaded only the SCAT5, and three (IJF, WAKO, WKF) provided only medical-rule recommendations such as suspension periods. Table 2 shows six steps for eight organisations and five for FIBA, and initial rest was 24-48 hours in most; World Rugby required one week of relative rest for adults and two weeks for children (each including 24 hours of complete rest), and boxing required a 30-day suspension before step 2. Minimum time to return after a single concussion ranged from 5 days (FIBA) to 180 days (WAKO, loss of consciousness over one minute), resistance training began at step 3 or step 4, and FIFA, IIHF and World Rugby allowed accelerated pathways.
paper.limitations: The review depends on publicly available documents from one date, and the authors note that no organisation answered requests for supplementary material. The narrative text says eight organisations require six steps but names seven (Table 2 lists eight, including IFAF), and the discussion says IFAF and WR lacked a 24-48 hour rest period while FIBA's is listed as 24 hours. The paper uses the CISG statement as its benchmark without assessing how any protocol performs in practice, and it describes itself as a commentary.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff working with athletes in combat, contact or collision sports should identify which return-to-play protocol their governing body uses, since minimum return times and resting requirements vary widely. Where a sport has no published protocol, the paper recommends the 2023 CISG framework, which includes starting the first step within 24 hours, health-care clearance before collision-risk activity, and cognitive assessment alongside symptoms.
paper.athleteDev: The paper addresses return to play rather than training design. Its performance-relevant point is that sport-specific drills and intensities should be specified at each RTP step, which the authors find in detail only in the FIFA protocol, with FIBA and IBA giving brief examples.
paper.rtp: This is the paper's full subject. It shows which steps, resting periods and clearance points each organisation requires, but it does not establish a safe return date for any athlete. The authors argue that minimum return times should follow current evidence and that accelerated pathways, such as those in FIFA, IIHF and World Rugby, rest on symptom reports the paper describes as low in reliability.

records.sourceFile: Comprehensive Analysis of Prohibited Substances and Methods in Sports - Unveiling Trends, Pharmacokinetics, and WADA Evolution.pdf

paper.citation: Oleksak P, Nepovimova E, Valko M, Alwasel S, Alomar S, Kuca K. Comprehensive Analysis of Prohibited Substances and Methods in Sports: Unveiling Trends, Pharmacokinetics, and WADA Evolution. Environmental Toxicology and Pharmacology. 2024. Journal pre-proof.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers the substances and methods on the 2023 WADA Prohibited List, organised by list section, with pharmacokinetic and metabolite notes and a summary of adverse analytical findings reported from 2003 to 2021. Anabolic agents were the most common class of findings, followed by stimulants and diuretics and masking agents. The authors also outline the history of anti-doping testing and the role of WADA.
paper.tldr: This review maps the 2023 WADA Prohibited List by section and summarises which substances were most often reported in doping tests from 2003 to 2021. It is useful for orientation, but it does not measure health or performance effects in athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the 2023 WADA Prohibited List, with sections on each list category, pharmacokinetic and metabolic notes, and tables and charts of adverse analytical and atypical findings from WADA annual reports (2003 to 2021). The text does not describe a systematic literature search.
paper.findings: Anabolic agents (S1) made up 49.5% of reported findings from 2003 to 2021, with testosterone (40.6%), stanozolol (11.0%) and nandrolone and 19-norsteroids (10.0%) the most common S1 compounds. Stimulants (12.1%) and diuretics and masking agents (8.7%) were the second and third most common sections, and no non-approved substance (S0) finding was reported. The authors state that the implementation of the Steroidal Module of the Athlete Biological Passport in 2014 'significantly affected' laboratory reports, seen as a marked fall in testosterone findings.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how the literature was searched or selected, so coverage of individual substances is not reproducible. Counts of findings depend on testing volume, detection methods, list revisions (for example clenbuterol moving from S3 to S1 in 2006) and the COVID-19 pandemic, which the authors say affected 2020 and 2021. The authors note eight-finding discrepancies between WADA summary tables and resolved them by using the tables of identified substances.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the section structure of the Prohibited List and the review's description of therapeutic use exemptions as orientation when a medication or supplement may contain a prohibited substance. The list is updated every year, so decisions should be checked against the current list rather than this 2023 summary, and the finding counts do not show how often athletes use each substance.
paper.athleteDev: The review helps staff understand which substance classes are prohibited and how they are classified, which supports education on clean-sport rules. It does not assess training methods or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It describes prohibited substances and anti-doping testing, not injury treatment, rehabilitation or the timing of return to play.

records.sourceFile: Concussion Guidelines Step 2 -   Evidence for Subtype Classification.pdf

paper.citation: Lumba-Brown A, Teramoto M, Bloom OJ, Brody D, Chesnutt J, Clugston JR, et al. Concussion Guidelines Step 2: Evidence for Subtype Classification. Neurosurgery. 2019;0:1-12.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pools prevalence of five concussion subtypes (cognitive, ocular-motor, headache/migraine, vestibular and anxiety/mood) and sleep disturbance within 3 days of injury, and compares concussed patients with controls. Headache/migraine and cognitive subtypes were the most prevalent in children and adults respectively, and adults were more likely than controls to show cognitive, vestibular and anxiety/mood subtypes. Cognitive symptoms were worse than in controls in both age groups, and cervical strain could not be analysed.
paper.tldr: Pooled acute data show that headache, vestibular, cognitive and mood features are common within 3 days of concussion, and that cognitive symptoms are worse than in controls. The authors recommend subtype assessment at the first clinical contact, but the evidence is mostly symptom reports from a small number of studies.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA and MOOSE guidance, searching MEDLINE, SCOPUS, Cochrane registers, PsycINFO and SPORTDiscus for English-language studies published 1990 to 2017. Studies of concussed patients with clinical evaluation within 3 months were included, and the acute analyses used assessments within 0 to 3 days, pooling proportions, prevalence ratios against uninjured or baseline controls, and standardized mean differences with random-effects models, Egger tests and trim-and-fill adjustment.
paper.findings: Ten studies gave prevalence data and 15 gave symptom or test data. Headache/migraine (0.52, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.67) and vestibular (0.50, 0.40 to 0.60) were the most prevalent subtypes in children, and cognitive (0.40, 0.25 to 0.55) was most prevalent in adults. Adults with concussion were 4.4, 2.9 and 1.7 times as likely as controls to show the cognitive, vestibular and anxiety/mood subtypes, and cognitive symptoms were higher than in controls in children (SMD 0.66) and adults (SMD 0.24), with vestibular symptoms higher in both groups (SMD 0.18 and 0.36).
paper.limitations: Several analyses rest on very few studies, for example 2 studies for the pediatric sleep disturbance SMD, and no cervical strain study met inclusion criteria. Publication bias was suspected for some pooled estimates, the sample is mainly North American sport concussion, and the search end date is November 2017 in the abstract but July 2017 in the methods. The text also conflicts internally: the Discussion calls headache/migraine the most common subtype in adults although Table 3 shows cognitive (0.40) above headache/migraine (0.38), and the ocular-motor SMD of 0.72 is assigned to adults in the abstract and Table 5 but to pediatric patients in the Results text.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can screen for cognitive, vestibular, headache, mood and sleep symptoms at the first encounter after concussion, since these features were common within 3 days of injury. The authors recommend assessing all five subtypes and sleep disturbance early, but the paper does not show that subtype-specific management improves outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the paper is a reminder that cognitive, vestibular and mood symptoms can be present early after a head impact and should be flagged to medical staff. It does not evaluate training or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The paper does not study return to play. Its subtype assessment within 3 days of injury may inform the first evaluation, but it reports no recovery trajectories and cannot set return-to-play timing, which the authors say will be reported in a later step.

records.sourceFile: Concussion and the sleeping brain.pdf

paper.citation: Donahue CC, Resch JE. Concussion and the Sleeping Brain. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:68.
paper.abstract: This review proposes that the concussion neurometabolic cascade and neuroinflammation alter sleep-wake physiology through noradrenaline, glymphatic clearance and extracellular ion changes. Sleep disturbance is common after concussion and is associated with longer symptom resolution and recovery in adolescents and adults. The authors conclude that sleep should be assessed across baseline, acute and later recovery, although no evidence-based sleep management guidance yet exists.
paper.tldr: Sleep changes after concussion are common and are linked to slower symptom resolution, and this review proposes a physiological model for why. The model is theoretical, so it should guide questions about sleep assessment rather than treatment decisions.
paper.methods: Narrative review with a theoretical model, drawing on the sleep and concussion literature. The paper does not describe a systematic search, study selection or quality appraisal.
paper.findings: The authors report that up to 70% of concussed people endorse sleep changes, and that sleep disturbance is associated with more symptoms and longer symptom resolution. In one study of adolescents aged 11 to 18, reporting sleep symptoms was linked to up to a fourfold increase in recovery time, and in high school and collegiate athletes less than seven hours of sleep before computerized neurocognitive testing was associated with more reported symptoms and with slower reaction times and lower ImPACT memory scores.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, and its mechanistic model is an interpretation that has not been tested. The cited studies differ widely in timing after injury (from the first 48 h to years later), sample and sleep measure, and the authors state that research on sleep and concussion is still in its infancy.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can ask about sleep at baseline and after injury, because sleep changes are common and linked to slower recovery. The review gives no validated sleep assessment or management protocol: the authors note that no validated concussion-specific sleep guidelines exist and that the SCOAT sleep questions come from a questionnaire not yet validated in concussed people.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the practical message is to protect sleep before baseline neurocognitive testing, since poor sleep can lower test scores. The review does not evaluate training or performance interventions.
paper.rtp: The review links persistent sleep symptoms to longer recovery and suggests adding clinical sleep measures to the concussion management protocol, but it gives no criteria or timing for return to play. It should inform the sleep questions asked in a concussion protocol, not decide clearance alone.

records.sourceFile: Concussion with primary impact to the chest and the potential role of neck tension.pdf

paper.citation: Jadischke R, Viano DC, McCarthy J, King AI. Concussion with primary impact to the chest and the potential role of neck tension. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2018;4:e000362.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study tested chest impacts on a helmeted and unhelmeted crash-test dummy and reconstructed two NFL collisions that caused concussion. Helmeted impacts produced higher neck tension and head flexion, and the authors estimated upper cord and brainstem strain in the two cases.
paper.tldr: Helmet mass in chest-primary football impacts increased neck tension in a crash-test dummy. In two concussive NFL collisions, the authors estimated high cord and brainstem strain from combined neck tension and flexion, which is a proposed mechanism that needs further study.
paper.methods: A Hybrid III dummy was struck in the chest with and without a helmet at 5-10 m/s (test series 1). Two NFL game collisions were reconstructed on the same dummy, and a finite element head and neck model estimated cervical strain.
paper.findings: The helmeted dummy had 40% +/- 10% higher upper neck tensile force (t=9.84, p<0.001) and 8% +/- 3% higher head flexion angle (t=7.267, p<0.001) than unhelmeted impacts of equal severity, with about 18% less head displacement and rotational velocity. In the two reconstructions, neck tension was 2646 N (case A) and 1342 N (case B), and estimated cord and brainstem strain was 13.0%-18.6% and 8.7%-12.2% from combined tension and flexion.
paper.limitations: Two cases is a very small sample, and the dummy is not human, so tissue strain was estimated rather than measured. The model was not validated for brainstem or spinal cord tissue, the 0.65 coupling ratio rests on limited data, and in case A the facemask also appears to have contacted the other player's helmet. The abstract gives 10%-20% strain and states that strain 'is a factor in concussion', while the body reports 13.0%-18.6% and 8.7%-12.2% (Table 3 simple sums are 14.4%-20.5% and 10.1%-14.1%) and frames neck tension as a possible mechanism needing further research.
paper.practicalImplications: Helmet mass added to the head can raise neck tension in chest-primary impacts, so chest-to-chest impacts should be considered alongside head-to-head impacts when evaluating helmets. Neck tension should be treated as a candidate mechanism, not an established concussion measure.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not address training or performance. Its relevance is to equipment design, since helmet mass increased neck tension in dummy chest impacts.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions for an individual athlete. It offers no clinical test, threshold or clearance criterion, and its two case reconstructions do not establish a diagnostic or prognostic standard.

records.sourceFile: Consensus statement on concussion in sport - The 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport - Amsterdam, October 2022.pdf

paper.citation: Patricios JS, Schneider KJ, Dvorak J, Ahmed OH, Blauwet C, Cantu RC, et al. Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;57:695-711.
paper.abstract: This consensus statement from the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport summarises evidence and expert recommendations on concussion prevention, assessment, management, return to learn and sport, and long-term effects. It introduces updated sideline and office assessment tools.
paper.tldr: After a suspected concussion, remove the athlete and do not return them that day unless an experienced clinician has evaluated them. Use a multimodal assessment of at least 10-15 minutes, relative rest for up to 48 hours, then a graded return to learning and sport with written clearance.
paper.methods: Expert panel of 31 members voted anonymously on recommendations at the October 2022 conference and follow-up meeting, using an 80% majority as consensus. Recommendations were informed by 10 systematic reviews, and the statement reports dissent alongside the votes.
paper.findings: Mouthguard use was associated with a 28% lower concussion rate in ice hockey, and a policy disallowing body checking in child and adolescent ice hockey reduced game concussions by 58%. Limiting contact practice in American football was associated with a 64% reduction in practice-related concussions. Prescribed subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise within 2-10 days was reported as effective for reducing persisting symptoms, and unrestricted return to sport typically occurs within 1 month (pooled mean 19.8 days, 95% CI 18.8 to 20.7, 57 studies, I-squared 99.3%).
paper.limitations: The authors state that the statement reflects evidence available at the conference, will need updating, and is not a prescriptive standard. Evidence is limited for para athletes, females, preadolescents and children aged 5-12, and the SCAT6 and SCOAT6 still require validation. The definition of concussion did not reach 80% agreement, and the expert panel had limited demographic and geographic diversity. Several authors disclose paid or unpaid roles with leagues and sport bodies.
paper.practicalImplications: Remove any athlete with suspected concussion and do not return them to play that day unless an experienced clinician has evaluated them. Allow at least 10-15 minutes for a multimodal off-field assessment, and do not rely on neurocognitive scores alone for management or clearance.
paper.athleteDev: Performance and sport science staff should not use baseline or neurocognitive scores in isolation to clear an athlete for training. The statement supports mouthguards in child and adolescent ice hockey and neuromuscular warm-ups in rugby, but it gives no performance training prescription.
paper.rtp: Return to sport follows six steps: symptom-limited activity, aerobic exercise, individual sport-specific exercise, non-contact drills, full-contact practice, then full game play. Each step typically takes at least 24 hours, and athletes should not begin any at-risk activity until symptoms and clinical findings have resolved. Unrestricted return requires written readiness from a healthcare professional under local rules, and the statement gives no fixed day count.

records.sourceFile: Context Matters- Revisiting the First Step of the ‘Sequence of Prevention’ of Sports Injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Bolling C, van Mechelen W, Pasman HR, Verhagen E. Context Matters: Revisiting the First Step of the 'Sequence of Prevention' of Sports Injuries. Sports Medicine. 2018;48:2227-2234.
paper.abstract: This review argues that sports injury prevention should describe the injury problem in its context, using the socioecological model. The authors propose qualitative research methods as a way to explore injury context before preventive measures are designed.
paper.tldr: Injury prevention work often describes the injury problem without context, which can produce interventions that work in controlled settings but not in practice. The authors propose exploring the athlete's context with qualitative methods before designing an intervention.
paper.methods: Conceptual review. The authors revisit the four-step sequence of prevention, draw on the socioecological model, and cite prior reviews, a RE-AIM review and a survey of teams. No systematic search or formal appraisal of sources is described.
paper.findings: The authors argue that the first step, describing the injury problem, has mostly been done without considering context, which may help explain the limited real-world effect of efficacious interventions. They cite a systematic review of 52 injury prevention trials using the RE-AIM framework, which identified major gaps in the adoption and maintenance of interventions. They also cite the Nordic Hamstring Survey, in which teams did not adopt an exercise programme with well-documented effects on injury and re-injury risk and kept using exercises with little supporting evidence.
paper.limitations: This is a conceptual argument, and the proposed qualitative approach is not tested for its effect on injury outcomes. Its claims rest on selected literature and analogy, and no search method is reported.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff planning an injury prevention program should describe the injury problem in context, including the athlete, sport, setting and coach or organizational factors, before choosing an intervention. The authors suggest qualitative work with athletes, coaches and health providers as a way to do this, but present it as a research approach rather than a tested staff procedure.
paper.athleteDev: The paper addresses injury prevention rather than performance. Its relevance to performance is the authors' point that an exercise program with good efficacy may not be adopted by teams, so staff should consider how athletes and coaches will use a program in their own setting.
paper.rtp: This paper does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. It concerns injury prevention and should not be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Core muscle injury - Evaluation and treatment in the athlete.pdf

paper.citation: Forlizzi JM, Ward MB, Whalen J, Wuerz TH, Gill TJ IV. Core Muscle Injury: Evaluation and Treatment in the Athlete. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022:1-9.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of core muscle injury in athletes, covering pathoanatomy, history and examination, imaging, nonoperative rehabilitation, and operative treatment and return to play. It draws on a literature search and the senior author's experience with professional, collegiate and elite athletes.
paper.tldr: Core muscle injury is a clinical diagnosis to consider in any athlete with inguinal pain, and adductor or hip pathology often coexists. Structured rehabilitation is the first step, and surgery with mesh and a relaxing myotomy is considered after persistent symptoms despite 12 weeks of nonoperative care.
paper.methods: Narrative and literature review. The authors state that a comprehensive literature search identified studies on diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation, and that the senior author's experience was compared with established treatment algorithms. No databases, dates or inclusion criteria are reported.
paper.findings: The authors state that pain proximal to the inguinal ligament, with tenderness at the rectus abdominis insertion, is highly suggestive of core muscle injury, that adductor longus tendinopathy is not uncommon, and that MRI may underestimate the extent of injury. Cited rehabilitation evidence includes a single-blinded randomized trial in which active rehabilitation produced more pain-free return to play than conventional therapy (13/20 vs 3/20). Cited surgical outcomes include 90% return to sport at 3 months after surgery versus 27% with physical therapy in a randomized trial, and an 89% return-to-play rate in 27 hips treated for combined hip and core pathology.
paper.limitations: The review states that evidence in this field is lacking and that large comparative studies of operative techniques have not been done. Many outcomes come from small or heterogeneous series, and several recommendations reflect the senior author's practice.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should consider core muscle injury in any athlete with groin pain above the inguinal ligament, and check the adductor longus for coexisting injury. Nonoperative rehabilitation of about 2 to 3 months, progressing to sport-specific work, is the first step, and the authors advise surgical referral after 12 weeks of persistent symptoms.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not measure performance. It notes that persistent groin pain can limit athletic performance, and that core strengthening and postural balance are central to nonoperative care.
paper.rtp: The review gives return-to-play timelines of about 4 weeks for isolated sports hernia repair and about 12 weeks when an adductor release is added. The authors' return criteria are healed wounds, full painless hip range, painless adductor activity and resolved preoperative groin pain, but these timelines reflect their protocol and small series, so they are reference points rather than validated criteria.

records.sourceFile: Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction Years After Cessation of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Use.pdf

paper.citation: Bulut Y, Rasmussen JJ, Brandt-Jacobsen N, Frystyk J, Thevis M, Schou M, et al. Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction Years After Cessation of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Use. JAMA Network Open. 2024;7(12):e2451013.
paper.abstract: In 90 men in recreational strength training, impaired myocardial flow reserve measured by rubidium-82 PET/CT was more frequent in men with current or former anabolic androgenic steroid use than in controls. Among former users, longer accumulated duration of use was associated with higher odds of reduced flow reserve. The authors conclude that impaired coronary microcirculation may persist after AAS use ends.
paper.tldr: Men who used anabolic steroids had more impaired coronary microvascular function on PET imaging than men who had never used them, including former users years after stopping. Longer cumulative use was linked to worse flow reserve among former users, although the sample was small.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study following STROBE reporting. Men aged 18 years or older in recreational strength training were grouped as current AAS users, former users (at least 4 weeks of use and stopped at least 3 months earlier), or controls with no AAS use. Use was checked with urine testing, and myocardial flow reserve was measured with rest and adenosine stress rubidium-82 PET/CT.
paper.findings: Impaired MFR below 2.0 occurred in 6 of 32 current users (18.8%) and 1 of 31 former users (3.2%), and in none of 27 controls (overall P = .02); the adjusted pairwise comparison of current users vs controls was not significant (P = .08). MFR below 2.5 occurred in 9 current users (28.1%), 8 former users (25.8%) and 1 control (3.7%) (overall P = .02), with nonsignificant pairwise comparisons (current vs control P = .05; former vs control P = .09). Mean MFR did not differ significantly between groups (P = .15). Among former users, each doubling of accumulated AAS duration was associated with MFR below 2.5 (odds ratio 2.1, 95% CI, 1.03-4.35; P = .04), and time since cessation was not.
paper.limitations: The primary outcome, mean MFR, did not differ significantly between groups, and post hoc pairwise comparisons were not significant; the authors say the sample was not large enough for prevalence comparisons with multiple-comparison adjustment. Group allocation relied on self-report, and urine testing detected AAS in 3 participants (10%) classed as former users. Selection bias cannot be excluded, the design cannot show causation, and the groups differed in blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, body fat and illicit drug use, which the authors treat as potential confounders.
paper.practicalImplications: When an athlete or trainee reports past or current AAS use, staff could treat coronary microvascular health as a possible concern that may persist after stopping and refer for cardiology assessment. The paper cannot quantify an individual's risk or define a screening protocol.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not test training outcomes. Its relevance to performance is indirect: it suggests that supraphysiologic AAS use in strength-trained men may carry cardiovascular risk that persists after cessation, which matters for athletes who use these drugs.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The study enrolled men without established cardiovascular disease and did not study injured athletes, so it cannot clear anyone for return to sport or judge cardiac fitness after AAS use.

records.sourceFile: Cryotherapy for treating soft tissue injuries in sport medicine - A critical review.pdf

paper.citation: Racinais S, Dablainville V, Rousse Y, Ihsan M, Grant ME, Schobersberger W, et al. Cryotherapy for treating soft tissue injuries in sport medicine: a critical review. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: The authors found no human evidence that cryotherapy limits secondary injury or improves tissue regeneration, and they rely largely on animal studies. Cryotherapy may be recommended in the first 6 hours after injury to reduce pain and possibly haematoma, but it should be used with caution beyond 12 hours because animal studies suggest it may interfere with healing. More human research is needed.
paper.tldr: Human evidence supports cryotherapy only for short-term pain relief, with no proven healing benefit. Animal studies suggest icing may delay muscle regeneration after large injuries, though it may help limited injuries, so the authors advise caution with continued use beyond the first hours.
paper.methods: Critical review with a structured search of Medline and Web of Science without automatic filters, using combined terms for cryotherapy, soft tissue and injury. Records were screened by two reviewers against criteria covering acute muscle, tendon or ligament injury, cryotherapy compared with a control, application only after injury, original research and English language. Of 452 records screened, one human and 26 animal studies were eligible, and the authors synthesized them with clinical literature.
paper.findings: The single human study, a pilot trial in gastrocnemius tears, did not show a difference between cryotherapy and control in pain, functional recovery or convalescence time; the authors note that an RCT able to detect a 10 percent difference in full recovery would need 396 participants. Among 25 animal muscle studies, cryotherapy reduced early swelling, microvascular permeability and some inflammatory markers, but several studies reported delayed necrotic fibre removal, smaller regenerating fibres and slower regeneration after large injuries, while repeated icing of a limited injury in rats facilitated recovery. The only tendon study reported 46 percent and 51 percent reductions in prostaglandin E2 in patellar and Achilles tendons within 3.5 hours.
paper.limitations: The human evidence base is one pilot study, and the sample was too small to detect differences. Animal injury models, cooling methods and outcome measures varied widely, and the authors note that cooling temperatures reached in animals may not be achievable in humans. The authors declare no competing interests.
paper.practicalImplications: Cryotherapy may be used for pain relief in the first hours after an injury, but staff should not present it as healing treatment. The authors advise caution with continued cryotherapy beyond the early hours, since animal studies suggest it may interfere with regeneration. Staff should set expectations that the evidence for protocols on timing, duration and temperature is not yet available.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not address performance. The authors do note that a reduction in pain could in theory allow earlier and more aggressive rehabilitation, but they state that no evidence currently supports this.
paper.rtp: The review concerns acute soft tissue injury management and does not study return to sport. Its advice to limit cryotherapy beyond the first hours is a caution about tissue healing and cannot be used to set return-to-play timing.

records.sourceFile: Cryotherapy induces an increase in     muscle stiffness.pdf

paper.citation: Point M, Guilhem G, Hug F, Nordez A, Frey A, Lacourpaille L. Cryotherapy induces an increase in muscle stiffness. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2017;1-7.
paper.abstract: Ten healthy volunteers underwent four 4-minute sets of air-pulsed cryotherapy (-30°C) over the gastrocnemius medialis, with 1-minute recovery between sets. Muscle temperature fell, and shear modulus measured by ultrasound elastography rose: +11.5% after the second set, +34.7% at 30 minutes and +25.4% at the end of a 40-minute follow-up. Ankle passive torque and EMG amplitude did not change, and the authors attribute the stiffness increase to a temperature-driven change in the tissue rather than to muscle activation.
paper.tldr: Cold air applied to the calf made the muscle measurably stiffer on ultrasound elastography, and the change lasted at least 40 minutes after treatment. Passive ankle torque did not change, and no injury or performance outcome was measured.
paper.methods: Ten healthy volunteers lay prone with the right ankle at 0°. Air-pulsed cryotherapy (-30°C) was applied to the gastrocnemius medialis in four 4-minute sets, and shear modulus, muscle temperature, passive torque and EMG were recorded at baseline, during treatment and for 40 minutes afterward. Two participants' EMG and torque data were lost, and repeated-measures ANOVA was used.
paper.findings: Muscle temperature fell by 6.1 ±1.8°C at the end of treatment and reached its lowest point 9 minutes after treatment (-7.1 ±1.0°C). Shear modulus rose by +11.5% after the second set (P=.011), +34.7% at 30 minutes (P<.001) and +25.4% at the end of follow-up (P<.001). Passive torque (P=.878) and EMG amplitude (P=.871) showed no significant change.
paper.limitations: The design was single-group with no control condition or washout, so reversibility could not be tested. The sample was ten healthy volunteers. The temperature probe was not guided by ultrasound, so temperature and stiffness were not measured from exactly the same tissue.
paper.practicalImplications: Cold air applied to the calf may leave the muscle stiffer for at least 40 minutes. For return to play immediately or within 40 minutes of cryotherapy, the authors advise avoiding it on strain-prone muscles and locations or following it with a progressive, specific warm-up. These are the authors' recommendations drawn from a single-group stiffness study, not outcome-tested guidance.
paper.athleteDev: Cryotherapy before performance work may leave the calf muscle stiffer for about 40 minutes, but passive torque did not change. No sprint, jump, strength or other performance measure was taken, so this paper does not show a performance effect.
paper.rtp: After cryotherapy, the authors suggest a progressive, specific warm-up before return to activities that load muscle, and avoiding cryotherapy in strain-prone muscles. The study measured stiffness only, in healthy volunteers, and cannot show that these steps reduce strain or reinjury.

records.sourceFile: DOESST~1.PDF

paper.citation: Alvacite Cardenas D, Preston N. Does strengthening the cervical spine musculature enhance neck strength and reduce sports-related concussions in rugby and football players? A systematic literature review. J Bodyw Mov Ther. 2025;45:332-358.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis searched seven databases from January 2002 to September 2022 for neck strengthening studies in rugby and football players, with 10 studies and 3,453 players included. Two male rugby trials (3,125 players) showed fewer concussions with programmes that included neck strengthening (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.92). No study showed a concussion benefit in football or female rugby players, and neck strength gains were seen mainly in rugby neck extension.
paper.tldr: In two trials of male rugby players, injury-prevention programmes that included neck strengthening were linked to roughly half the concussion rate, but no included study showed this in football or female players. Do not assume the rugby result transfers to other groups or reflects neck work alone.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review registered with PROSPERO, searching seven databases (2002 to September 2022) and trial registries for RCTs and cohort or pre-post studies of cervical strengthening in rugby and football players. Risk of bias was assessed by the primary author with CASP and, for RCTs, RoB 2; seven RCTs were pooled in RevMan with random-effects models, and GRADE was used for certainty.
paper.findings: Two rugby RCTs (3,125 players) gave a pooled concussion risk ratio of 0.55 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.92), about 14 fewer concussions per 1,000 players than the 30 per 1,000 control rate. Across five RCTs (191 players), no pooled neck strength plane differed significantly; in subgroups, rugby neck extension favoured strengthening (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.24, P = 0.04), while football neck flexion (SMD -0.73) and extension (SMD -0.55) favoured the control group. Total neck strength (SMD 1.3, 95% CI -0.05 to 2.65, P = 0.06) did not reach significance.
paper.limitations: Only two male rugby trials inform the concussion result; both used multicomponent movement-control programmes and are rated at high risk of detection bias, yet GRADE certainty is rated High, and Table 3 gives Hislop et al. a concussion RR of 0.72 (90% CI 0.51 to 1.0, P = 0.11). The discussion calls the non-significant total neck strength result significant, the abstract counts eight neck-strength studies while the results pool five, the stated age range differs (12 to 26 in results, 7 to 26 in discussion), and the PROSPERO number differs between abstract (CRD4202236054) and methods (CRD42022360574). The 'football' subgroup includes female Australian football players.
paper.practicalImplications: For male rugby players, the review supports including neck strengthening within an injury-prevention or strength programme, which can be done in the field, since two trials of such programmes were linked to fewer concussions. For football and female players, the evidence shows no concussion benefit and no consistent strength gain, so programmes should not be presented as concussion prevention. The authors suggest neck strength and imbalance screening to identify higher-risk athletes, but this was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: Neck strength gains were seen mainly in rugby neck extension, in trials running about 5 to 14 weeks, which may matter for contact positions. The review did not measure sport performance, and its total neck strength result did not reach statistical significance.
paper.rtp: The review does not study return to play or rehabilitation after concussion or neck injury. Its suggestion that neck strength could guide return-to-play decisions comes from the authors' citation of earlier work and was not tested here.

records.sourceFile: Deceleration training in team sports - Another potential vaccine for sports-related injury.pdf

paper.citation: McBurnie AJ, Harper DJ, Jones PA, Dos'Santos T. Deceleration Training in Team Sports: Another Potential 'Vaccine' for Sports-Related Injury? Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: This Current Opinion article reviews the biomechanical and physiological features of horizontal deceleration in team sports. It links these features to injury mechanisms and offers considerations for assessing, training and monitoring deceleration. The authors propose that deceleration be treated as a key performance indicator alongside sprinting.
paper.tldr: Horizontal decelerations are frequent in team sports and load the body in a distinct way. The authors argue they should be assessed, trained and monitored like sprinting, but the injury benefit of training them is not yet shown.
paper.methods: Narrative review. No search strategy is described. The authors synthesise biomechanical, physiological and injury literature and summarise proposed mechanisms in a table.
paper.findings: The authors report that high-intensity decelerations occur more often than equally intense accelerations in several team sports, and produce high impact peak forces, loading rates and eccentric demands. They cite Jaspers et al. finding that higher cumulative deceleration loading over 2 to 4 weeks led to increased overuse injury risk. They report that two field-based 6-week multidirectional speed interventions, with deceleration drills in the early weeks, reduced surrogates of ACL injury risk and improved change-of-direction performance.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review without a described search or quality appraisal. The authors state that the link between decelerations and injury is not clearly established, and the long-term injury effect of deceleration training is unknown. Several mechanistic points come from laboratory and animal studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider adding a deceleration capacity test to athlete testing batteries, alongside linear speed and jump tests. Track high-intensity decelerations alongside sprinting and high-speed running, and periodise their exposure. These are the authors' recommendations and are not yet tested for injury outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: The authors recommend that field testing of deceleration capacity and technique be included in testing batteries in the same way as linear speed and jump testing, and that deceleration ability and deceleration-focused resistance training be developed progressively within multidirectional speed programmes. These are untested recommendations, not trial results.
paper.rtp: The paper gives no return-to-sport criteria or data from injured athletes. It can inform the idea of progressive deceleration exposure, but it cannot be used to set a return-to-play threshold or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Development of a preliminary multivariable model predicting hamstring strain injuries during preseason screening in soccer players - A multidisciplinary approach.pdf

paper.citation: Baize D, Mériaux-Scoffier S, Massamba A, Hureau T, Reneaud N, Garcia-Gimenez Y, et al. Development of a preliminary multivariable model predicting hamstring strain injuries during preseason screening in soccer players: a multidisciplinary approach. Annals of Medicine. 2025;57(1):2494683.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort study built a preliminary logistic regression model to predict hamstring strain injuries from preseason screening in French soccer players. The model combined personal, psychological, sprint and knee-flexor fatigability measures. It identified 79% of players who were later injured in this sample, but it has not been externally validated.
paper.tldr: A short preseason screen combining personal, psychological and sprint-fatigue measures identified most players who later had a hamstring strain in this sample. The model is preliminary and untested in a separate group, so it should not yet be used to decide who is at risk.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort during the 2022 preseason. The text reports 122 participants from five French clubs, with 2 excluded for knee pain and 120 analysed. Players completed psychological, nutrition, sleep and burnout questionnaires, had isometric knee flexor and extensor torque measured, and performed ten 30-m sprints with photocells, radar and video, with knee-flexor torque retested after the sprints. Injuries were self-reported monthly and cross-checked with club staff, and variables were screened by univariate tests and entered into Wald backward stepwise logistic regression, with 200 bootstrap resamples for internal validation.
paper.findings: Twenty-nine players (24%) sustained at least one HSI. The final eight-variable model included sex, age, HSI history, best sprint time, post-sprint knee-flexor torque change, maximal theoretical velocity (V0), squared perceived vulnerability and subjective norms, with an AUC of .815 (95% CI .719 to .912), sensitivity 79.3% and specificity 75.6%. Injured players had a larger post-sprint knee-flexor torque loss than uninjured players (-11.7% vs -4.8%), and this was the only significant modifiable predictor (OR .48, 95% CI .27 to .84); female sex was also significant (OR 9.61, 95% CI 1.15 to 80.74), while HSI history (OR 2.81), age (OR 1.43), best sprint time, V0 and the psychological variables were not significant at p < .05.
paper.limitations: The authors state the model needs external validation and that event-per-predictor recommendations were not reached, so overfitting is possible. Imputation was 14.2% for force-velocity variables, including V0, and 9.0% for running kinematics. Sample counts conflict in the source: the text reports 22 female and 100 male participants before 2 exclusions, while Table 3 lists 22 female and 98 male among the 120 analysed; the abstract also describes the sample as regional and national players although Table 2 lists 6 international players. The authors describe the female subgroup as small and the model as most applicable to young male players.
paper.practicalImplications: The model uses two psychological questionnaires and one repeated-sprint test with knee-flexor torque before and after, which the authors describe as a short preseason screen. Because the model is preliminary and untested externally, use it as a research prompt alongside clinical judgement rather than to exclude players from training. The authors propose testing whether targeted prevention for flagged players reduces injuries.
paper.athleteDev: In this sample, injured players lost more knee-flexor torque after repeated sprints, and players with faster best sprint times tended to have higher odds (OR .44, not significant), while the V0 association was also not significant. Post-sprint hamstring torque loss is a candidate monitoring marker, but the evidence comes from one preliminary, unvalidated model.
paper.rtp: The study predicts a first hamstring strain in players screened without a current injury or hamstring pain. It does not address recovery, return to play or re-injury, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions or post-injury loading.

records.sourceFile: Different anatomic patterns of the indirect tendon of the rectus femoris.pdf

paper.citation: Mechó S, Iriarte I, Lisbona R, Pérez-Andrés R, Pruna R, Rodríguez-Baeza A. Different anatomic patterns of the indirect tendon of the rectus femoris. Surg Radiol Anat. 2024.
paper.abstract: This cadaver study dissected 48 hemipelves to describe anatomical variants of the indirect tendon of the rectus femoris proximal tendinous complex. Superior and inferior aponeurotic expansions and an unusual myotendinous junction origin were common, and four indirect tendon patterns were defined, three of them complex. The authors suggest complex patterns may stiffen the tendon and act as non-modifiable risk factors for rectus femoris injury.
paper.tldr: About 60% of 48 cadaver specimens had variants of the rectus femoris indirect tendon, and the authors classify four patterns. Any link to injury risk in athletes is a hypothesis, not a finding.
paper.methods: Standardized anterior-to-posterior dissection of 48 embalmed hemipelves with thigh from donors aged 54 to 98 years. Variants were recorded as frequencies and percentages, and associations with sex and side were tested with Pearson chi-square (P < .05).
paper.findings: Variants were found in 29 of 48 specimens (60.4%): inferior aponeurotic expansion in 23 (47.9%), superior expansion in 21 (43.7%; more than one in 6 of these) and an unusual myotendinous junction origin in the free portion of the indirect tendon in 19 (39.6%). Based on the expansions, patterns were standard in 19 (39.6%), superior and inferior complex in 15 (31.2%), inferior complex in 8 (16.7%) and superior complex in 6 (12.5%). No variant was associated with sex or side (P = .25 to .85).
paper.limitations: Specimens came from elderly donors, not athletes, and only one hemipelvis per donor was studied without the full lower limb. Stiffness and injury risk were not measured, and the authors state they speculate on the biomechanics and propose MRI or ultrasound studies to confirm the link.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians reading proximal rectus femoris imaging can expect superior or inferior expansions of the indirect tendon in many people, as described here. The authors' suggestion to screen athletes for complex patterns and target them with prevention programs is untested.
paper.athleteDev: This study cannot guide training or performance decisions. It describes tendon anatomy in elderly cadavers and did not test athletes or prevention programs.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not study injured athletes, healing or re-injury, and the proposed role of complex tendon patterns in rectus femoris injury is unconfirmed.

records.sourceFile: Dilemma in the Treatment of Sports Injuries in Athletes - Tendon Overuse  Muscle, Muscle Strain, and Tendon Rupture.pdf

paper.citation: Kjær M, Petersen J, Dünweber MR, Andersen JL, Engebretsen L, Magnusson SP. Dilemma in the Treatment of Sports Injuries in Athletes: Tendon Overuse, Muscle Strain, and Tendon Rupture. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2025;35:e70026.
paper.abstract: This special issue article reviews current treatments for tendon overuse injury, acute muscle strain and tendon rupture in athletes. Although evidence-based prevention and treatment exist, incidence remains high and single treatments give only partial recovery. The authors highlight unresolved dilemmas in each injury type.
paper.tldr: Strength training with reduced sport load is the best-supported treatment for tendinopathy. Muscle strain and Achilles rupture still leave athletes with incomplete recovery, and the best timing, type of rehabilitation and return-to-sport criteria remain unresolved.
paper.methods: Narrative review of published trials, meta-analyses and clinical studies on tendinopathy, acute hamstring and calf strain, and Achilles tendon rupture. The authors do not describe a systematic search or inclusion criteria.
paper.findings: For tendinopathy, loading therapies outperform non-loading care, benefit was kept when strength training intensity was cut from 80 to 90% to 55% 1RM, and limiting sport to a self-monitored pain level of 2 to 5 out of 10 did not limit improvement. For acute hamstring strains, progressive eccentric strengthening with graded running gave the fastest return to play and the lowest re-injury rate in a cited review, and one study found that each extra day before return lowered re-injury risk by about 1.5%. After Achilles tendon rupture, both surgery and nonoperative care lead to tendon elongation (longer with nonoperative care), and greater elongation is linked to poorer function.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, and many of its specific estimates come from single studies or small trials. Several key questions, such as how much sport-specific training to allow and when to return elite athletes to sport, are listed as unresolved rather than answered.
paper.practicalImplications: For tendinopathy, use progressive strength training with a reduction in sport load rather than rest alone, and do not expect PRP, oral NSAIDs or injected IGF-I to add benefit to strength training. For acute hamstring strain, use progressive eccentric and running rehabilitation; the clinical tests and MRI features linked to re-injury in one study are risk markers, since the authors state that how to judge tissue readiness remains unknown. For Achilles rupture, the authors suggest elite athletes may benefit more from surgery because of tendon elongation, while noting that the optimal treatment is unresolved.
paper.athleteDev: In elite athletes, adding strength training on top of full training without reducing sport load had no benefit in one cited trial, while pain-monitored sport at 2 to 5 out of 10 did not slow recovery. How much sport-specific training to keep during heavy loading is unresolved, so set it case by case.
paper.rtp: For hamstring-type strains, the review supports graded eccentric and running rehabilitation, and reports that a longer return-to-play period lowers re-injury risk, based on one study. For Achilles rupture, it shows that functional deficits persist after surgery or nonoperative care, and it does not give a validated return-to-sport standard for elite athletes.

records.sourceFile: Disabled throwing shoulder-elbow players have high rates of impaired foot function.pdf

paper.citation: Nagamoto H, Kimura R, Hata E, Kumai T. Disabled throwing shoulder/elbow players have high rates of impaired foot function. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: In 91 baseball players with a disabled throwing shoulder or elbow, impaired foot function was found in 83 (91%) and floating toes in 74 (81%). Of the players with impaired foot function, 73 (88%) also had floating toes, and of those with floating toes, 73 (99%) had impaired foot function; both associations were statistically significant (P < 0.001).
paper.tldr: Among 91 young baseball players with a disabled throwing shoulder or elbow, most had impaired foot function (91%) and floating toes (81%), and the two findings usually occurred together. The study cannot show whether foot dysfunction contributes to the injury.
paper.methods: Retrospective observational study of 91 male baseball players aged 12 to 17 years diagnosed at one outpatient clinic with a disabled throwing shoulder or elbow. Foot function was tested with a rock-paper-scissors toe movement test, and floating toes were recorded when no toe touched the mat in standing. Associations were tested with chi-square tests.
paper.findings: Impaired foot function was found in 83 of 91 players (91%) and floating toes in 74 (81%). Of the 83 with impaired foot function, 73 (88%) had floating toes, compared with 12% of those without impaired function (P < 0.001). Of the 74 with floating toes, 73 (99%) had impaired foot function, compared with 59% of those without floating toes (P < 0.001).
paper.limitations: There was no control group, the design is retrospective, and the study is from one clinic, so causation and generalisation cannot be shown. The Methods state that 167 players diagnosed at the clinic were included, while the Results report 91 who met the inclusion criteria; the exclusion criteria (foot function not evaluable, history of foot injury) are listed but the number excluded for each is not reported. Floating toes were not analysed by toe or by throwing side, footwear was not recorded, and one examiner did all assessments, which removes inter-rater error but leaves examiner bias unaddressed (Inference).
paper.practicalImplications: A simple foot check (the rock-paper-scissors toe test and a standing check for floating toes) can be added to the assessment of a thrower with shoulder or elbow pain, since most players in this sample showed both findings. The paper does not show that the findings cause injury, so they should be recorded as observations, not treated as the cause. Staff should note that the authors call for controlled studies before foot training is assumed to reduce injury.
paper.athleteDev: No performance outcome was measured. Staff working with young baseball players may use the two foot tests as part of a movement screen, but the paper does not show that the tests predict throwing performance or change after training.
paper.rtp: The study assessed players once, at the clinic visit, and did not follow them through rehabilitation or back to throwing, so it cannot show whether restoring foot function changes return-to-throw outcomes. The authors state that future studies are needed to test whether improving foot function affects injury occurrence.

records.sourceFile: Do healthy athletes exhibit at-risk biomechanics for anterior cruciate ligament injury during pivoting movements.pdf

paper.citation: Di Paolo S, Bragonzoni L, Della Villa F, Grassi A, Zaffagnini S. Do healthy athletes exhibit at-risk biomechanics for anterior cruciate ligament injury during pivoting movements? Sports Biomechanics. 2022.
paper.abstract: Thirty-four healthy competitive pivoting-sport athletes performed a frontal deceleration and a 90 degree change of direction, measured with wearable inertial sensors. An at-risk trial, defined as at least five of nine ACL risk factors present at once, occurred in 9% to 12% of trials; 24 athletes (71%) showed the profile in at least one trial. Higher approach speed (OR 4.3) and female sex (OR 4.8) were significantly associated with the profile.
