paper.tldr: A multi-joint pattern similar to the ACL injury mechanism was common in healthy pivoting-sport athletes during cutting and deceleration, and was linked to higher approach speed and female sex. The study has no injury outcome, so it shows occurrence of the pattern, not injury risk.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 34 healthy competitive athletes (18 men, 16 women; mean age 22.8 years) in soccer, rugby and basketball, performing three valid trials per leg of a frontal deceleration and a 90 degree change of direction. Full-body kinematics came from 15 wearable inertial sensors at 60 Hz, and nine risk factors were assessed at initial contact and maximum knee flexion. Logistic regression tested sex, limb dominance, age and approach speed, and SPM1D compared knee moment waveforms.
paper.findings: Of 398 valid trials, the at-risk profile occurred in 9.0% at maximum knee flexion and 12.1% at initial contact, with no significant difference by task or frame. Twenty-four athletes (71%) showed the profile in at least one movement and 5 (15%) in at least three. In the change-of-direction model at maximum knee flexion, approach speed (OR 4.3, 95% CI 1.6 to 11.7) and female sex (OR 4.8, 1.2 to 19.8) were associated with the profile, and at-risk trials showed greater knee abduction, flexion and rotation moments over parts of stance.
paper.limitations: The 5-of-9 threshold is arbitrary, as the authors acknowledge, and the frontal and transverse cut-offs came from this cohort's quartiles, so the rate is partly sample-specific. Four regression models were built but only the change-of-direction model at maximum knee flexion fit significantly, trials from the same athlete were pooled, and there was no injured or ACL-reconstructed comparison group or injury outcome. Only two pre-planned tasks were studied, and kinematics came from wearable sensors rather than marker-based capture.
paper.practicalImplications: A multi-joint screen of this kind can show how often an athlete moves in patterns resembling the ACL injury mechanism, and the authors recommend testing at game-like speeds because faster approaches were linked to the profile. Results support awareness and screening, not labelling athletes as high ACL risk, because the cut-offs are not validated against injury.
paper.athleteDev: Faster approach speed was associated with the at-risk profile and with the authors' description of a performance and injury-risk conflict in cutting. The paper does not test any technique intervention, so it cannot show whether changing these patterns lowers injury rates or affects cutting performance.
paper.rtp: The study did not include injured or ACL-reconstructed athletes, and the authors state that the profile's sensitivity in reconstructed athletes is unknown. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions, although the authors suggest future studies in reconstructed athletes.

records.sourceFile: Does acute fatigue negatively   affect intrinsic risk factors of the lower extremity injury risk profile -   A systematic and critical review.pdf

paper.citation: Verschueren J, Tassignon B, De Pauw K, Proost M, Teugels A, Van Cutsem J, et al. Does Acute Fatigue Negatively Affect Intrinsic Risk Factors of the Lower Extremity Injury Risk Profile? A Systematic and Critical Review. Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of whether acute fatigue changes prospectively identified modifiable intrinsic risk factors for lower extremity injury in healthy athletes or physically active people; 43 studies reported relevant fatigue effects and 8 matched all extraction criteria. The authors report that acute fatigue can decrease single-leg postural control, ankle joint position sense and isokinetic hamstring and quadriceps strength and can affect hamstring to quadriceps ratios, and conclude that it alters lateral ankle sprain, patellofemoral pain and hamstring injury risk profiles.
paper.tldr: Acute fatigue lowers some tests linked to patellofemoral pain and hamstring injury risk, such as isokinetic quadriceps and hamstring strength, and broader evidence suggests it worsens single-leg balance. The evidence comes from few, small, mostly male studies with no injury outcomes, so it supports testing athletes in a fatigued state, not predicting injury from one test.
paper.methods: Systematic review registered with PROSPERO and reported to PRISMA-P, searching PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro and the Cochrane Library to 29 May 2019, plus reference lists. Eligible studies used an acute fatigue protocol in healthy athletes or physically active people and measured an outcome identified as a significant prospective injury risk factor, excluding children, older adults, pregnant women and injured populations. Two authors screened records independently, and the Cochrane risk of bias tool was applied to included studies.
paper.findings: Of 68 full texts assessed, 43 studies reported acute fatigue effects on modifiable risk factors, and 8 matched all extraction criteria. Quadriceps concentric peak torque at 60 degrees/s decreased in all three studies that measured it (significant in two), and hamstring concentric (one study) and eccentric normalized (one study) strength decreased; hamstring to quadriceps ratios fell in one of four studies at 60 degrees/s and one of three at 180 degrees/s. Ankle joint position sense decreased in one study (n = 72) but not another (n = 19), and no included study used the original postural control measures, although the wider set of 29 studies predominantly showed decreased single-leg postural control.
paper.limitations: Only eight studies met the criteria, with high risk of bias and mainly male soccer players, and no meta-analysis was possible. Only 4 of the 8 studies reported the time from fatigue to testing. Table 3 lists the Cohen et al. eccentric hamstring test at 60 degrees/s while Table 4 lists 120 degrees/s, and the text says seven women were included in one study while Table 4 gives six.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors advise that functional testing and injury risk profiling should include a fatigued condition, since single tests give only a snapshot. They suggest tracking each athlete's fatigue response (for example percentage decline or absolute test decrement) over a season rather than relying on group averages. Record the fatigue protocol and the time from fatigue to testing, which only 4 of the 8 included studies reported.
paper.athleteDev: The review suggests fatigue reduces balance, stability and strength measures that matter in sport, so performance staff may track these tests late in sessions or matches. The authors cite a higher injury rate late in matches and training, which they link to fatigue, but they do not test that link.
paper.rtp: The review excludes injured populations and does not assess rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions, so it cannot inform them. The authors say fatigue-based profiling could be applied to rehabilitation and return to sport, but that has not been tested.

records.sourceFile: Does muscle-tendon unit structure predispose to hamstring strain injury during running - A critical review.pdf

paper.citation: Huygaerts S, Cos F, Cohen DD, Calleja-González J, Pruna R, Alcaraz PE, Blazevich AJ. Does Muscle-Tendon Unit Structure Predispose to Hamstring Strain Injury During Running? A Critical Review. Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: A critical review of how biceps femoris long head muscle-tendon architecture, fibre type and innervation may predispose the muscle to strain injury during running. The authors conclude that the evidence is insufficient to confirm any single mechanism and that prospective and imaging studies are needed.
paper.tldr: Hamstring strain injury most often involves the biceps femoris long head, and differences in its architecture may explain some of the individual risk. The proposed mechanisms are not yet confirmed, so they should not be used alone to identify at-risk athletes.
paper.methods: Critical narrative review of anatomical, architectural, fibre-type and innervation evidence for the biceps femoris long head and its relation to hamstring strain injury during sprint running. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: Isolated injury to the biceps femoris long head is the most common acute hamstring strain in intermittent running sports, most often during sprinting (51% of cases). The authors report that fascicles are longer and pennation greater in the proximal and middle sections, which may increase strain. They cite Timmins et al. as finding that professional soccer players with fascicles shorter than 10.6 cm had about fourfold higher injury risk. Evidence on fibre type and innervation is inconsistent, and no single mechanism is confirmed.
paper.limitations: The authors note that current evidence is largely from imaging, modelling, cadaveric and small cohort studies. Ultrasound fascicle length estimates required large (over 60%) extrapolation and can be altered by light pressure on relaxed muscle, and no prospective study has tested whether these structural features cause injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who assess hamstring risk may record biceps femoris long head structure where measurement is available, but should treat it as one risk factor within a wider profile. Prospective data are needed before structure-based screening or targeted training decisions are made.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this review does not support a training prescription. It suggests that eccentric and strength-endurance hamstring work is a plausible way to reduce risk, with the mechanisms still unconfirmed. Monitoring fascicle length or architecture is a research-stage option rather than a validated screen.
paper.rtp: This review does not give return-to-sport criteria. It addresses injury predisposition in healthy running athletes and does not test whether fascicle length, pennation or fibre type should guide the timing of return after a hamstring strain.

records.sourceFile: Doping prevalence among US elite athletes subject to drug testing under the World Anti-Doping Code.pdf

paper.citation: Davoren AK, Rulison K, Milroy J, Grist P, Fedoruk M, Lewis L, et al. Doping Prevalence among U.S. Elite Athletes Subject to Drug Testing under the World Anti-Doping Code. Sports Med Open. 2024;10:57.
paper.abstract: An anonymous survey of U.S. elite athletes in the USADA testing pool (n = 1,398 analysed) estimated that 6.5 to 9.2% had used a prohibited substance or method without a TUE in the past 12 months. Category-level use ranged from 0.1% to 4.2%, with in-competition cannabinoids the most common.
paper.tldr: About 7 to 9 in 100 U.S. elite athletes in this anonymous survey reported using a banned substance or method in the past year, with cannabinoids the most common. The figure is self-reported and depends on how inconsistent answers are handled.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional anonymous web survey of athletes in the USADA Olympic and Paralympic testing pool, administered through Qualtrics by an independent research team (April to June 2020). Direct questions covered each WADA Prohibited List category without a TUE over the past 12 months, with validation and consistency items. Two prevalence calculations were made. Of 2,616 athletes in the sampling frame, 1,398 were analysed after exclusions.
paper.findings: Overall prevalence was 9.2% (n = 128) by the first method and 6.5% by the second. Category prevalence ranged from 0.1% (diuretics or masking agents; stem cell or gene editing) to 4.2% (in-competition cannabinoids), and 1% reported asthma inhalers beyond the allowable dose. Of those who reported doping, 84.4% reported one category. Athletes who reported doping were younger (mean 26.4 vs 28.1 years, p = 0.008); prevalence did not differ by sex, competition level or sport risk category.
paper.limitations: Self-reported and anonymous, so under-reporting and social desirability bias are possible. Some respondents gave inconsistent answers, and 31 were excluded for failing validation items, although the authors state that the prevalence rates were identical when these athletes were included. Non-response may bias the estimate, and the survey was taken at the start of COVID-19 competition stoppages. Sport was not asked directly, and only 53.4% of the targeted population (1,398 of 2,616) gave usable responses.
paper.practicalImplications: Anti-doping education and detection may need to focus on specific categories, especially in-competition cannabinoids and asthma inhalers used beyond the allowable dose, rather than on doping in general. Staff can use these category-level results when discussing medication use, TUEs and in-competition rules with athletes, but the figures should not be read as a measure of an individual team or sport.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: staff working with athletes in competitive environments may use these findings to raise awareness of cannabinoid and inhaler rules during in-competition periods. The results are population estimates and cannot identify doping in any named athlete.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed elite athletes about past doping behaviour and did not assess injury, medical treatment or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Doping prevalence in competitive sport - Evidence synthesis with best practice recommendations and reporting guidelines from the WADA working group on doping prevalence.pdf

paper.citation: Gleaves J, Petróczi A, Folkerts D, de Hon O, Macedo E, Saugy M, et al. Doping Prevalence in Competitive Sport: Evidence Synthesis with "Best Practice" Recommendations and Reporting Guidelines from the WADA Working Group on Doping Prevalence. Sports Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: A systematic review of 105 studies (102,515 surveyed athletes) found doping prevalence in competitive sport ranging from 0 to 73%, with most estimates under 5%. The authors rated the quality of the evidence as mostly moderate or low and published best-practice reporting recommendations.
paper.tldr: Doping prevalence estimates in competitive sport come from weak and inconsistent studies, and the reported figures range widely. The authors recommend standard survey wording, defined timeframes and clear reporting of athlete level and sport.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review and evidence synthesis with no time restriction. Studies with prevalence data (survey or sample analysis) from competitive athletes were included. Two quality tools were developed (QUAD-SRP for self-report surveys and QUAD-SAP for sample analysis), and studies were graded high, moderate or low. Results were synthesised descriptively, because data were too inconsistent for meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Of 105 studies, 89 used self-reported surveys and 17 used sample analysis (one used both). Prevalence ranged from 0 to 73%, with most under 5%. Quality ratings were 20 high, 60 moderate and 25 low. Among the 17 sample-analysis studies, only 3 were rated high. Ten studies used randomized response technique surveys. Ten of the 20 high-rated studies reported 0 to 5%, while the single highest-scoring randomized response study reported 43.6 to 57.1%. The authors say that higher figures should not be assumed to be closer to the truth without considering method and population.
paper.limitations: Heterogeneous studies that differed in substances, timeframes, populations and reporting, so meta-analysis was not possible. The U.S. (26 studies) and a few sports (for example weightlifting and cycling) dominate the evidence, and many countries and sports have none. Quality criteria were developed for this review. Counts are internally inconsistent: the abstract gives 17 sample-analysis studies and 35 countries with 12 international studies, while the Results text gives 34 countries with 15 international studies and the Discussion refers to 10 and to nine sample-analysis studies.
paper.practicalImplications: When reading doping prevalence figures, check the substance list, timeframe, population and whether therapeutic use exemptions and inadvertent positives were handled. Treat the 0 to 73% range as evidence of wide methodological variation, not as a sport or team estimate. The authors' recommendations on defining doping, asking about behaviour in a defined period, and reporting athlete level and sport are a reasonable checklist for staff reviewing anti-doping survey work.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this review does not give a doping estimate for a specific sport, position or level, so it cannot inform team-level planning. It is most useful for judging how strong a doping prevalence claim is before it is used in an anti-doping or education discussion.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It covers doping prevalence in competitive athletes and does not address injury, rehabilitation or medical clearance.
